The authors show that posttranslational myristoylation of VP4 plays a critical role in this process. Using computer simulations of VP4 and its interactions with the membrane, the authors show that myristoylated VP4 anchors to the membrane faster, aggregates faster to form dense phases via LLPS, and remodels the membrane, thereby lowering the energy barrier for the protein to insert into the membrane. The authors further showed, through simulations, that the myristoylated VP4 forms helices within the membrane with higher stability, which then form structured pores, disrupting the membrane and enabling the transfer of the viral genome into the host cell.
Strengths:

The strength of the manuscript is that different sets of unbiased and enhanced-sampling simulations using all-atom and coarse-grained models of the protein and membrane are performed to bridge multiple time and length scales involved in the transfer of the viral genome into the host cell. There is experimental support for most of the conclusions arrived at from the simulations.
Weaknesses:
The drawback is that experimental evidence was lacking to support the pore-formation proposal from the simulations.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for summarizing the strengths of our work and for correctly identifying the drawback that no direct experimental evidence supports the pore- formation proposal from the simulations. Such a drawback is a field-wide open question in the functional study of viral VP4-like proteins, and as stated in our Section 3.5, While the ability of picornaviral VP4 proteins to form size-selective membrane pores is well-documented, the atomic-level structure of these pores remains unknown. Against this background, while we proposed the pore-formation model and explored it with simulations, we used cautious language when reporting our data, emphasizing that the pore-forming insights from our simulations suggest potential roles of MYR.

Nevertheless, gaining an experimentally determined atomic structure of the VP4 pore (if it indeed arises from such pores) would definitely broaden our in silico findings here, and we would be thrilled to see such evidence emerge.

disp-quote.p: Although the paper is well written, some clarifications are needed in the simulation methods, and typos should be fixed.

(1) On page 5, section 2.2, on atomistic molecular dynamics simulations of isolated VP4, please mention the size of the simulation box used, rather than just the water buffer distance. The protein in this case is disordered. How were the simulation box dimensions chosen.

body.p: Thank you for the comment. We have clarified in the Methods section that, after applying a 12 Å water buffer, the simulation box has dimensions of 98.852 Å × 98.852 Å × 98.852 Å. This box size was determined by the initial full-length VP4 structure, which was obtained via Swiss homology modeling using the crystallographically resolved VP4 structure in PDB 4GB3 as a template; applying the water buffer around this structure resulted in the indicated box dimensions.

disp-quote.p: (2) On page 5, section 2.3, Martini CGMD simulations of VP4-membrane interaction and VP4 condensation, it is mentioned that since the VP4 protein is disordered, the authors did not include any elastic networks in the protein. However, in the next sentence, the authors state that to reduce the conformational flexibility, different amounts of elastic networks are introduced. How did the authors choose the CG beads to introduce the elastic network? How are the pairs of beads ignored when the number of elastic bonds is reduced from 206 to 132?

body.p: Thank you for the questions, and we apologize for the missing details regarding the construction of the different VP4 Martini models. After carefully revisiting our MD setup, we confirmed that the VP4-partial and VP4-rigid models were not constructed by gradually introducing elastic bonds into a bond-free VP4 model, but rather by using a partially resolved VP4 crystal structure and a fully MD-relaxed VP4 structure, respectively. Specifically, for the VP4-partial model (which has 132 elastic bonds), the bead pairs involved in the elastic bonds were determined using the full-length VP4 structure obtained via Swiss homology modeling based on the partially resolved VP4 crystal structure in PDB 4GB3. The default Martini elastic bond criteria, with lower and upper elastic bond cutoffs of 0.5 and 0.9 nm, respectively, were used, resulting in 132 elastic bonds. For the fully rigid VP4 model, the fully relaxed VP4 structure from the atomistic MD simulation of VP4 was used to determine the elastic bonds, resulting in a total of 206 bonds using the same cutoffs. The newly updated details regarding the construction of the VP4-partial and VP4-rigid models do not alter the interpretations of the simulation data obtained using these models. We have changed the text in the revised manuscript accordingly.

disp-quote.p: (3) On page 5, section 2.3, "amount" is written as "mount"

body.p: Thanks for your careful reading of our manuscript, and we have corrected this typo.

disp-quote.p: (4) Was the pressure on the membrane applied in all three directions or only in the x and y-directions?

body.p: Thank you for the comment. We apologize for the inaccurate description regarding the pressure in the XY direction in the original manuscript. After carefully verifying our simulation setup, we confirmed that to prepare a planar lipid bilayer, a harmonic bias potential was initially applied to the lipid headgroups of the bent membrane, constraining them to a common Z-plane to achieve structural planarity. Subsequently, to maintain membrane planarity during the PMF calculations, a weak harmonic position restraint was applied exclusively along the Z-axis to the membrane. By constraining only the Z-axis while allowing lipid molecules to diffuse freely within the XY-plane, this setup effectively preserved the intrinsic lateral fluidity of the lipid bilayer while ensuring structural planarity throughout the free energy simulations. Accordingly, we have revised Figure S11 and updated its accompanying caption to reflect this methodology accurately. The updated figure have been incorporated into the revised manuscript.
